name: Castor oil beard

lead: Castor oil is a thick plant oil pressed from Ricinus communis seeds. People apply it to the jaw and cheeks hoping for denser facial hair, and it also leaves hair looking glossier.

Proponents say it improves follicle circulation or moisture. No study has tested it for beard growth, and a general reference says no high-quality studies show it stimulates follicle growth or density. Beard growth depends largely on androgens such as DHT and on genetics.

paras: People rub a small amount into the beard area, often as a nightly routine alongside other beard care, usually for months. Claims circulate mainly on social media and hair-care forums.
Topical castor oil is generally considered low-risk, with rare contact dermatitis reported, especially undiluted. It is an over-the-counter cosmetic product.

angle.text: Users rub castor oil into the face hoping it thickens facial hair, and it conditions the hair so it looks glossier. Growth claims are widespread online; beard-specific studies were not found.

lead: Castor oil beard refers to the practice of massaging castor oil, a vegetable oil pressed from the seeds of Ricinus communis, into the jaw and cheeks in the belief that it thickens or fills in facial hair. Followers apply it to patchy areas hoping for a denser, fuller beard, and the oil also leaves hair and skin looking conditioned. Castor oil is about 90 percent ricinoleic acid and has a long history of medicinal and cosmetic use, mainly as a laxative and an emollient.[1] Because it conditions the skin and hair, it is also an ingredient in beard oils, which are sold to keep beards soft, shiny and manageable.[2]

A general reference work on castor oil says it is promoted online for hair, lash and brow growth.[3] A 2022 systematic review of 22 articles on coconut, castor and argan oil for hair found weaker evidence for castor oil, limited to improving hair luster, and no strong evidence for growth.[4] No beard-specific study of castor oil was found. Beard growth is understood to be driven largely by androgens, especially dihydrotestosterone, and to be partly genetic.[5]
infobox: Claimed to thicken or fill in beard hair
Some beard oils and hair-care blends[2]

paras: Castor oil is a colorless to pale yellow oil from castor seeds, which contain 40 to 60 percent oil. Its fatty acids are mostly ricinoleates, and the hydroxyl group on ricinoleic acid makes it more polar than most vegetable oils.[1] It appears in the Ebers Papyrus (about 1550 BC) as a laxative, and today is used in cosmetic creams as an emollient.[1]

Online hair-care communities and social media promote castor oil for thicker hair, lashes and brows, with proponents citing improved follicle circulation or moisture retention.[3] A general encyclopedia entry on castor oil describes these as folk and social-media claims and reports that reviews find at most weak or indirect evidence that it improves hair luster, by coating strands and reducing dryness-related breakage.[3] That entry has no beard-specific content.[3]

Beard growth in men begins at puberty and is stimulated by dihydrotestosterone, with growth rate and density partly genetic.[5] No source reviewed describes a mechanism by which a topical oil would change this.

sections.h: Use in beard oils and grooming
paras: Wikipedia's beard-oil article lists castor oil among the ingredients used in beard oils, alongside jojoba, argan, coconut, grape seed, hempseed and ostrich oils, which address itching, dryness and sensitive skin by moisturising the beard and the skin beneath it.[2] It describes the appearance benefits as softer, less brittle hair, a slight shine that makes a beard look healthier, and easier styling, and says that beard oils making therapeutic claims in the United States must be approved by the FDA.[2] Carrier oils form the bulk of such products, and essential oils added for scent are typically diluted because they can irritate the skin on their own.[2]

In this framing castor oil's direct effect is cosmetic: a thick oil that coats strands and smooths the skin, which can make a patchy beard look more even. The separate claim that it increases the number or thickness of beard hairs is the one for which no study was found.

Topical use is generally regarded as low-risk. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review has deemed castor oil safe in leave-on products and patch tests show minimal irritation, though rare contact dermatitis has been reported, especially with undiluted use.[3] Case reports describe its thick texture contributing to hair felting.[3] Castor seeds contain the toxin ricin, but it is deactivated during oil extraction.[1]

sections.h: Research on castor oil and hair
paras: The 2022 Journal of Drugs in Dermatology review of coconut, castor and argan oil for hair in skin of color patients concluded that coconut oil has clinical evidence for brittle hair and infestation, castor oil has weaker evidence for improving luster and no strong evidence for growth, and argan oil has no significant supporting evidence for growth or quality.[4]

A 2017 International Journal of Trichology case report describes a patient whose scalp hair matted immediately after applying coconut and castor oil, attributed by the authors to castor oil's high viscosity with long hair; the condition was reported as irreversible and the hair had to be cut.[6]

No studies found of castor oil for beard growth. A randomized, double-masked trial of 3% minoxidil lotion for beard enhancement has been published, which is a different topical treatment.[7] Castor oil's hair research consists of reviews and small studies in scalp hair, and a 2021 randomized trial of castor oil on the eyelids examined blepharitis, not hair growth.[3][4]

Wikipedia says awareness of beard-oil and beard-grooming products has grown as workplaces and industries have become more permissive of facial hair.[2] Castor oil's beard and brow reputation spreads mainly through social media and hair-care forums, according to the general reference entry on the oil, which describes the growth claims as folk and social-media claims.[3] Minoxidil is the topical agent with a published randomized beard trial, and is the comparison treatment most often discussed for beard enhancement.[7]
